concepts.name: Shashtilakshana: Canonical Rules of Hindu Iconography in Stone
key_dimensions: Definition and textual sources (Shilpashastra, Manasara, Mayamata) governing proportions and postures
Distinction between Shashtilakshana and Chausath Kala — trap zone for overlapping terms
How canonical rules differ across Nagara, Dravida, and Vesara traditions
UPSC trap: Which text is associated with which regional tradition (e.g., Manasara vs. Mansollasa)

concepts.name: Nagara vs. Dravida vs. Vesara: Stone Carving Vocabulary Differences
key_dimensions: Structural elements exclusive to each style: Shikhara vs. Vimana vs. hybrid forms
Regional distribution and key temple examples where stone carving style is the identifier
Decorative motifs unique to each: Amalaka, Kalasha, Kudu arch, Gavaksha
UPSC trap: Vesara is often misidentified — its geographic and stylistic boundaries are contested

concepts.name: Mathura School of Stone Carving: Characteristics and Distinctives
key_dimensions: Use of spotted red sandstone from Sikri quarries — material as an identifier
Indigenous vs. Hellenistic influence debate compared to Gandhara school
Iconographic innovations: first standing Buddha, Bodhisattva typology
Chronological overlap with Kushana patronage and how it differs from Gupta-period Mathura

concepts.name: Gandhara School of Stone Carving: Greco-Buddhist Synthesis
key_dimensions: Material distinction: grey schist and stucco vs. Mathura's red sandstone
Hellenistic, Roman, and Iranian influences — specific stylistic markers (wavy hair, toga-like drapery)
Geographic extent: modern Pakistan/Afghanistan — geopolitical relevance in current affairs
UPSC trap: Comparing which school first anthropomorphized the Buddha — Mathura vs. Gandhara debate

concepts.name: Amaravati School of Stone Carving: Narrative Relief Tradition
key_dimensions: Use of white limestone (marble-like) — material as geographic and stylistic identifier
Narrative sculptural panels (Jataka stories) and dynamic movement as distinguishing feature
Influence on Southeast Asian stone carving traditions (Sri Lanka, Java)
UPSC trap: Amaravati Stupa carvings housed in multiple museums — Chennai Government Museum vs. British Museum controversy

concepts.name: Gupta Period Stone Carving: The 'Classical Ideal'
key_dimensions: Synthesis of Mathura and Gandhara elements into a distinctly Indian aesthetic
Key sites: Sarnath, Mathura, Udayagiri caves — site-to-period mapping
Stylistic markers: serene expression, clinging wet drapery, spiritual introspection
UPSC trap: Distinguishing Gupta-period sculpture from post-Gupta Pala school features

concepts.name: Hoysala Stone Carving: Soapstone (Chloritic Schite) Tradition
key_dimensions: Material advantage of soapstone (softness when quarried, hardening after exposure) enabling intricate detailing
Stellate/star-shaped platform (Jagati) as a Hoysala-exclusive architectural feature
Key sites: Belur, Halebidu, Somnathapura — UNESCO inscription status and significance
UPSC trap: Distinguishing Hoysala from Chalukyan stone carving — both in Karnataka with similar iconographic programs

concepts.name: Khajuraho Stone Carving: Erotic Iconography and its Theological Interpretation
key_dimensions: Chandela dynasty patronage and its political-religious context
Theological explanations: Shakta-Tantric symbolism, transition zone between worldly and divine (outer vs. inner sanctum)
Nagara sub-style classification: Khajuraho as a high point of the Chandela/Panchayatana Nagara variant
UNESCO World Heritage status and the oft-tested fact that erotic carvings cover only ~10% of total sculptures

concepts.name: Pallava Rock-Cut and Structural Stone Traditions: Mahabalipuram
key_dimensions: Distinction between rathas (monolithic rock-cut), mandapas (cave temples), and structural temples at the same site
Pancha Rathas: each ratha named after Pandavas but none actually used for worship — a common factual trap
Shore Temple as transition from rock-cut to structural tradition under Rajasimha
Bas-relief traditions: Arjuna's Penance / Descent of Ganga — world's largest bas-relief status and the interpretive debate

concepts.name: Odisha Stone Carving Tradition: Kalinga School
key_dimensions: Three orders of Kalinga architecture: Rekha Deul, Pidha Deul, Khakhara Deul and their stylistic carving programs
Konark Sun Temple: Chlorite stone use, erotic sculptures in cosmic/astronomical context
Lalitgiri, Ratnagiri, Udayagiri — Buddhist stone carving tradition in Odisha (often overlooked in favor of Konark)
UPSC trap: Distinguishing Odishan Nagara from North Indian Nagara — Odishan has unique Deul terminology not used elsewhere

concepts.name: Cave Temple Stone Carving Traditions: Ajanta, Ellora, Elephanta Compared
key_dimensions: Ajanta: exclusively Buddhist, painting-dominant but sculptural programs in later Mahayana caves
Ellora: multi-religious (Buddhist, Hindu, Jain) — chronological sequence and which caves belong to which religion
Elephanta: Shaiva iconography — Trimurti/Maheshmurti as the pinnacle of Rashtrakuta-era carving
UPSC trap: Kailasa Temple (Cave 16, Ellora) is a monolithic structural temple, NOT a cave — common misclassification

concepts.name: GI-Tagged Stone Carving Crafts: Living Traditions
key_dimensions: Makrana marble carving (Rajasthan) — same marble used in Taj Mahal, GI tag details
Odisha stone carving (Pattachitra stone vs. soapstone crafts) — artisan community (Silpakara)
Mahabalipuram stone carving — GI tag and UNESCO Creative City of Crafts and Folk Art status
UPSC trap: Distinguishing which stone carving traditions have GI tags vs. those that are only UNESCO-recognized

concepts.name: Buddhist Stupa Stone Railing and Torana Tradition
key_dimensions: Sanchi Stupa toranas: four gateways, narrative relief panels, yakshi bracket figures — patrons include artisans' guilds
Distinction between Sanchi, Bharhut, and Amaravati railing traditions — style and period differences
Aniconic vs. iconic representation of Buddha in early stupa carving — footprints, Bodhi tree, wheel as symbols
UPSC trap: Bharhut railings are now in the Indian Museum, Kolkata — not in situ, a common location-based question

concepts.name: Jain Stone Carving Traditions: Dilwara and Ranakpur
key_dimensions: Dilwara Temples (Mount Abu): Vimala Vasahi and Luna Vasahi — white marble, Solanki/Chaulukya patronage
Ranakpur Chaumukha Temple: 1,444 uniquely carved columns — no two columns identical (examinable superlative)
Jain iconographic program in stone: Tirthankaras, Shasanadevatas, and their distinguishing lakshanas
UPSC trap: Dilwara temples are often confused with Jaisalmer Jain temples — material (marble vs. yellow sandstone) is the differentiator

concepts.name: Medieval Islamic-Influenced Stone Carving: Sultanate and Mughal Adaptations
key_dimensions: Prohibition on figural representation leading to arabesque, geometric, and calligraphic stone carving styles
Pietra dura (Parchin kari) — inlay technique at Taj Mahal: technically stone inlay, not traditional carving
Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque: reuse of temple stone carving elements — spolia as a historical and architectural concept
UPSC trap: Fatehpur Sikri uses red sandstone while Taj Mahal uses white marble — material switch under Shah Jahan has an examinable rationale

concepts.name: Regional Stone Carving Traditions: Vijayanagara Empire
key_dimensions: Distinctive features: massive monolithic sculptures (Sasivekalu and Kadalekalu Ganeshas), narrative friezes
Hampi's Vitthala Temple stone chariot and musical pillars — acoustic properties as an examinable feature
Composite pillar tradition (Yali/Vyala columns) as a Vijayanagara signature
UPSC trap: Vijayanagara style is often confused with Hoysala — key differentiator is the use of granite vs. soapstone

concepts.name: Tribal and Folk Stone Carving: Memorial Stones and Megalithic Traditions
key_dimensions: Hero stones (Viragal/Virgal): commemorative stone carving tradition across Karnataka, Andhra, and Tamil Nadu
Sati stones (Satimata pillars): iconographic program and geographic distribution
Megalithic burial traditions: Menhirs, Dolmens, Cairn circles — Deccan and Northeast India distribution
UPSC trap: Megalithic traditions are prehistoric but hero stones are historical — overlapping terminology is a common exam trap

concepts.name: Conservation and Institutional Framework for Stone Carving Heritage
key_dimensions: ASI's mandate under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 (amended 2010) for protected stone monuments
UNESCO World Heritage Sites involving stone carving: criteria used (e.g., Mahabalipuram under criteria i, ii, iii, vi)
INTACH's role vs. ASI in conserving living stone carving craft traditions vs. monument conservation
UPSC trap: National Monuments Authority (NMA) was created by the 2010 amendment — its specific mandate vs. ASI's is a frequently tested distinction

concepts.name: Iconometric Texts (Shilpashastra) and their Regional Variants
key_dimensions: Key texts: Manasara (South India), Mayamata (Tamil tradition), Vishwakarma Prakash (North India), Aparajitapriccha (Gujarat)
Concept of Talamana (proportional grid system) in stone sculpture — how it controls carving outcomes
Distinction between Agamic texts (temple ritual focus) and Shilpashastra (craft/construction focus)
UPSC trap: Manasara is often assumed to be pan-Indian but is specifically a South Indian text — its attribution and regional scope is a high-frequency trap
